c-gift.text: Herodotus wrote that the Egypt reached by Greek ships was land 'acquired by the Egyptians, given them by the river', built up from its mud: the origin of the phrase 'the gift of the Nile'.
c-gift.label: consensus

c-nile-length.text: The Nile is about 6,650 km long.
c-nile-length.label: approx
c-nile-length.note: The figure depends on where the source is taken to be.

c-flood.text: The annual flood came from heavy summer rain on the Ethiopian highlands: at its peak the Blue Nile supplied almost 70 percent of the water, the Atbara more than 20 and the White Nile about 10.
c-flood.label: consensus

c-flood-timing.text: Before the modern dams, the flood reached Aswan in July and peaked at Cairo in October.
c-flood-timing.label: consensus

c-kemet.text: The flood left fertile black silt; Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land', and the desert Deshret, 'the red land'.
c-kemet.label: consensus

c-pliny-flood.text: Pliny recorded that a flood of 12 cubits meant famine, 14 gladness and 16 'unbounded transports of joy'; floods were measured on Nilometers.
c-pliny-flood.label: tradition
c-pliny-flood.note: A Roman writer of the 1st century CE.

c-two-lands.text: Upper (southern) Egypt and Lower (northern) Egypt had distinct cultures before unification, and kings were later called 'Lord of the Two Lands'.
c-two-lands.label: consensus

c-population.text: Karl Butzer estimated Egypt's population at about 0.9 million at unification, 1.6 million by 2500 BCE and 2.9 million under Ramesses II.
c-population.label: debated
c-population.note: No count of pharaonic Egypt's whole population survives; these are estimates of what the land could support. Others estimate 4-5 million for the New Kingdom.

c-naqada.text: The Naqada culture of Upper Egypt runs through three phases, from about 4000 to 3000 BCE.
c-naqada.label: approx

c-dee.text: Radiocarbon dating (2013) shows the Egyptian state formed faster than once thought: the Predynastic period began about 3800-3700 BCE, and King Aha came to the throne about 3111-3045 BCE.
c-dee.label: approx

c-uj.text: Tomb U-j at Abydos, about 3200 BCE, held small bone and ivory labels with signs recording goods and places, among the earliest Egyptian writing.
c-uj.label: debated
c-uj.note: Günter Dreyer, who found them, saw evidence for an independent and very early Egyptian invention of writing; others think Mesopotamia came first.

c-narmer.text: The Narmer Palette, about 3100 BCE, shows the king wearing the red crown of the north on one side and the white crown of the south on the other, smiting an enemy.
c-narmer.label: consensus

c-narmer-event.text: Whether the Narmer Palette records a real conquest is debated.
c-narmer-event.label: debated
c-narmer-event.note: Some see Narmer as the first known unifier; John Baines reads the scene as a ritual statement of kingship. Unification probably took several reigns.

c-menes.text: Later tradition credits a king called Menes with uniting Egypt and founding Memphis; which historical king, if any, he was is unknown.
c-menes.label: tradition

c-retainers.text: Kings of the 1st Dynasty were buried with servants killed to accompany them; a 2026 study found injuries at the time of death on 18 of 46 skulls from these graves.
c-retainers.label: debated
c-retainers.note: The evidence comes from the layout of the graves and from old, incomplete collections; the practice seems to end with the 1st Dynasty.

c-genome.text: The first whole genome from ancient Egypt (2025), of a man who lived about 2855-2570 BCE, shows about 80 percent North African and 20 percent eastern Fertile Crescent ancestry.
c-genome.label: approx

c-pharaoh-word.text: 'Pharaoh' comes from per-aa, 'great house', the palace; it was used for the king himself only from the New Kingdom.
c-pharaoh-word.label: consensus

c-titulary.text: A king had five official names, each introduced by its own title.
c-titulary.label: consensus

c-horus.text: The living king was identified with the god Horus and, in death, with Osiris.
c-horus.label: consensus

c-maat.text: Maat was the order of the universe established at creation, and also truth and justice; the king's task was to uphold it against chaos.
c-maat.label: consensus

c-divine-king.text: How divine Egyptians thought their king was is debated.
c-divine-king.label: debated
c-divine-king.note: Henri Frankfort stressed the king's divinity; Georges Posener countered him; John Baines sees the king as the manifestation of Horus in the palace, whose ordinary status was hardly that of a god.

c-sed.text: The Sed festival, known from the 1st Dynasty, renewed the king's powers, traditionally after 30 years of rule.
c-sed.label: approx

c-step.text: Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, about 2650 BCE, is the first pyramid and the first large building of stone in Egypt.
c-step.label: consensus

c-imhotep.text: Imhotep, an official of Djoser, is traditionally its architect; much later he was worshipped as a god of medicine.
c-imhotep.label: tradition
c-imhotep.note: His name and titles appear on a statue base of Djoser; the role of architect is tradition.

c-sneferu.text: Sneferu built or completed three pyramids, at Meidum (probably begun by his predecessor Huni) and Dahshur; the Bent Pyramid changes angle partway up, and the Red Pyramid was the first true pyramid completed.
c-sneferu.label: consensus

c-great-pyramid.text: The Great Pyramid of Khufu stood about 146 metres tall, with sides over 230 metres long that differ by only a few centimetres, and contains an estimated 2.3 million blocks.
c-great-pyramid.label: approx

c-tallest.text: It remained the tallest structure built by people for well over three thousand years, until a European cathedral spire surpassed it in the 13th or 14th century CE.
c-tallest.label: approx
c-tallest.note: Sources differ on which cathedral came first.

c-not-slaves.text: The pyramids were built not by slaves but by organised labour: perhaps 10,000 core workers on rotating shifts, fed by the state.
c-not-slaves.label: debated
c-not-slaves.note: That they were not slaves is the consensus; how voluntary the work was is debated. Mark Lehner calls it obligatory labour.

c-herodotus-pyramid.text: Herodotus, writing two thousand years later, said Khufu forced 100,000 Egyptians at a time to work on his pyramid for twenty years.
c-herodotus-pyramid.label: tradition

c-workers-town.text: Excavations since 1988 have uncovered the town of the pyramid builders south of the Sphinx, with bakeries, grain stores and barracks.
c-workers-town.label: consensus

c-merer.text: Papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf include the logbook of Merer, an official who shipped limestone from Tura to Giza by boat in Khufu's 27th year.
c-merer.label: consensus

c-ramps.text: How the blocks were raised is still debated: straight ramps, spiral ramps or other methods.
c-ramps.label: debated
c-ramps.note: A ramp with steps and post-holes of Khufu's time has been found at the Hatnub quarry.

c-ahramat.text: A 2024 study mapped a lost branch of the Nile running past the pyramid fields, which would have let boats bring materials close to the building sites.
c-ahramat.label: debated
c-ahramat.note: A proposal based on radar and cores; not yet widely tested.

c-corridor.text: In 2023 cosmic-ray imaging found a hidden corridor about 9 metres long above the Great Pyramid's entrance; its purpose is unknown.
c-corridor.label: consensus

c-sphinx.text: The Great Sphinx, about 73 metres long, was carved from the bedrock, probably for Khafre.
c-sphinx.label: approx

c-gods-egypt.text: Many Egyptian gods were linked with animals: Horus with the falcon, Hathor with the cow, Thoth with the ibis, Amun with the ram.
c-gods-egypt.label: consensus

c-ennead.text: The priests of Heliopolis taught that from the creator Atum came eight further gods, the Ennead, including Osiris, Isis and Seth.
c-ennead.label: consensus

c-osiris.text: No continuous Egyptian account of the Osiris myth survives; the fullest version is by the Greek writer Plutarch, about 120 CE.
c-osiris.label: consensus

c-soul.text: Egyptians thought a person had several spiritual parts, among them the ka, a life-force that received offerings, and the ba, which could leave the tomb by day.
c-soul.label: consensus

c-mummification.text: Embalming took about 70 days, and its quality depended on what a family could pay.
c-mummification.label: approx
c-mummification.note: Herodotus says 70 days in natron; modern accounts usually say 70 days for the whole process.

c-animal-mummies.text: Perhaps up to 70 million animals were mummified as offerings; scans show about a third of the wrappings contain no animal at all.
c-animal-mummies.label: approx

c-texts.text: The earliest religious texts written in a tomb are the Pyramid Texts of King Unas, about 2350 BCE; they were followed by the Coffin Texts and, in the New Kingdom, the Book of the Dead.
c-texts.label: approx

c-weighing.text: In Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead, the heart of the dead person is weighed against the feather of Maat, after a declaration of sins not committed.
c-weighing.label: consensus

c-democratisation.text: Scholars once held that an afterlife reserved for kings was 'democratised' after the Old Kingdom; many now argue that ordinary elites already hoped for one, and that what changed was writing it down.
c-democratisation.label: debated
c-democratisation.note: James Breasted proposed the idea in 1912; Mark Smith (2009) argues against it.

c-sign-counts.text: Egyptian scribes used over 1,000 hieroglyphs in the Old Kingdom and about 750 in the Middle Kingdom; Ptolemaic temple inscriptions used several thousand.
c-sign-counts.label: approx
c-sign-counts.note: Counts depend on how variant forms are counted; one estimate for the Ptolemaic period is up to about 8,000.

c-script-types.text: The script mixed signs for sounds, signs for whole words, and 'determinatives', unpronounced signs that showed what kind of word was meant; vowels were not written.
c-script-types.label: consensus

c-hieratic.text: Hieratic was a quick handwritten form of hieroglyphs; demotic, a still faster script, was used for everyday documents from about 700 BCE.
c-hieratic.label: consensus

c-literacy.text: Perhaps 1 percent of Egyptians could read and write in the third millennium BCE; estimates for later periods and particular places run from about 5 to 15 percent.
c-literacy.label: debated
c-literacy.note: John Baines's low estimate is widely cited; others argue the evidence is too thin to be sure, and literacy was higher in some communities.

c-satire.text: The 'Satire of the Trades', a Middle Kingdom school text, has a father praise the scribe's life and mock the hardships of other trades.
c-satire.label: consensus

c-rosetta.text: The Rosetta Stone records a decree of 196 BCE for Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek: three scripts, two languages. French soldiers found it in 1799.
c-rosetta.label: consensus

c-champollion.text: Thomas Young first showed that hieroglyphs could spell foreign royal names by sound; Jean-François Champollion announced the decipherment in 1822, showing that sound-signs and word-signs worked together.
c-champollion.label: consensus

c-pepi.text: The Old Kingdom ended after the unusually long reign of Pepi II.
c-pepi.label: approx
c-pepi.note: Contemporary texts record his 62nd and 65th years.

c-fip.text: In the First Intermediate Period (about 2160-2055 BCE) Egypt split between rival kings at Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south; Thebes won.
c-fip.label: approx

c-fip-drought.text: Whether drought caused the Old Kingdom's collapse is debated: Barbara Bell (1971) argued for failed Nile floods; Nadine Moeller argued that the famine texts are largely ideology and that the climate dried gradually.
c-fip-drought.label: debated
c-fip-drought.note: Moeller now sees the arid phase about 2200 BCE as 'just one factor' among several.

c-ipuwer.text: The 'Admonitions of Ipuwer', a poem describing Egypt turned upside down, survives in one later copy; scholars date its composition to the Middle Kingdom or later, not to the collapse itself.
c-ipuwer.label: debated
c-ipuwer.note: Older scholarship read it as an eyewitness account of the First Intermediate Period; John Van Seters argued for a still later date.

c-ipuwer-exodus.text: Some popular writers read Ipuwer's 'the river is blood' as a record of the Exodus plagues; Egyptologists generally reject this.
c-ipuwer-exodus.label: debated
c-ipuwer-exodus.note: Roland Enmarch, the poem's recent editor, finds the link unconvincing: the text is a literary lament of uncertain date, and it describes foreigners entering Egypt, not leaving.

c-mentuhotep.text: Mentuhotep II of Thebes, who became king about 2055 BCE, reunited Egypt during his reign, beginning the Middle Kingdom.
c-mentuhotep.label: approx

c-semna.text: Senusret III fixed Egypt's southern border at Semna, guarded by a chain of mud-brick fortresses such as Buhen, against the kingdom of Kush.
c-semna.label: consensus

c-fayum.text: Middle Kingdom kings developed farmland in the Faiyum basin and built pyramids at Lahun and Hawara.
c-fayum.label: consensus

c-classical.text: Middle Egyptian became the classical literary language; its works include the Story of Sinuhe and the Eloquent Peasant.
c-classical.label: consensus

c-hyksos.text: The Hyksos, from an Egyptian phrase meaning 'rulers of foreign lands', ruled northern Egypt from Avaris in the eastern Delta in the 17th-16th centuries BCE.
c-hyksos.label: consensus

c-avaris.text: Avaris had housed communities of people from the Levant since the late 12th Dynasty, many working for the crown; under the Hyksos it grew to about 250 hectares.
c-avaris.label: approx

c-stantis.text: A 2020 study of tooth enamel at Avaris found that many people had grown up outside Egypt before Hyksos rule began, suggesting the Hyksos rose from within rather than invading.
c-stantis.label: debated
c-stantis.note: One site, 75 individuals; the method cannot show where the newcomers came from. The later Egyptian tradition describes an invasion.

c-chariot.text: The Hyksos period is usually credited with bringing the horse and chariot and the composite bow to Egypt.
c-chariot.label: debated
c-chariot.note: Some horse remains may be earlier.

c-ahmose.text: Ahmose of Thebes, king from about 1550 BCE, took Avaris and drove out the Hyksos, founding the New Kingdom; the early 18th Dynasty later built a palace precinct there.
c-ahmose.label: approx

c-megiddo.text: In his 23rd year, about 1457 BCE, Thutmose III defeated a coalition at Megiddo after leading his army through a narrow pass; his annals at Karnak describe the campaign in detail.
c-megiddo.label: approx

c-empire.text: At its height the New Kingdom empire reached from beyond the Euphrates in Syria to beyond the Fourth Cataract of the Nile.
c-empire.label: consensus

c-hyksos-israel.text: The Egyptian priest Manetho, as quoted by Josephus, said the expelled Hyksos went on to found Jerusalem, and Josephus called them 'our forefathers'.
c-hyksos-israel.label: tradition

c-hyksos-israel-view.text: Most scholars do not equate the Hyksos with the Israelites, though some think distant memories of Hyksos movements may lie behind elements of the Exodus story.
c-hyksos-israel-view.label: debated
c-hyksos-israel-view.note: Manetho wrote over a thousand years after the events and survives only in quotation.

c-hatshepsut.text: Hatshepsut ruled as king, with full royal titles, from about 1473 to 1458 BCE, first alongside the young Thutmose III, and built the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri.
c-hatshepsut.label: approx

c-punt.text: Her temple shows an expedition to Punt bringing back myrrh trees, incense, gold, ebony and animals; Punt probably lay in the region of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia.
c-punt.label: debated
c-punt.note: The expedition is well documented; Punt's location is debated. A 2023 study of baboon mummies points to Eritrea and nearby regions.

c-defacement.text: Thutmose III later had Hatshepsut's images removed, but only some twenty years after her death, which makes simple revenge unlikely.
c-defacement.label: debated
c-defacement.note: Peter Dorman doubts revenge; Jun Yi Wong (2025) argues that much of the statue damage was ritual 'deactivation' also done to other kings.

c-akhenaten.text: Akhenaten (reigned about 1352-1336 BCE) made the Aten, the disk of the sun, the focus of worship, closed the temples of other gods, and built a new capital at Amarna.
c-akhenaten.label: approx

c-monotheism.text: Whether Akhenaten's religion was true monotheism is debated.
c-monotheism.label: debated
c-monotheism.note: Erik Hornung stresses that the king and queen shared in the divine; Jan Assmann sees a radical, exclusive break; others call Akhenaten a monotheist outright.

c-psalm104.text: The Great Hymn to the Aten has striking parallels with Psalm 104.
c-psalm104.label: debated
c-psalm104.note: That the parallels exist is agreed. Aaron Koller and others argue for direct borrowing; others see shared tradition or a common genre of praise.

c-nefertiti.text: His queen Nefertiti shared in the cult; her painted bust was found in a sculptor's workshop at Amarna in 1912.
c-nefertiti.label: consensus

c-amarna-letters.text: The Amarna letters, about 350 letters among 382 tablets, mostly in Akkadian cuneiform, record Egypt's correspondence with great kings and with its vassals in Canaan and Syria.
c-amarna-letters.label: consensus

c-habiru.text: Vassals such as the ruler of Jerusalem complained of the Habiru (Apiru), a class of outlaws and mercenaries; any link to the word 'Hebrew' is debated.
c-habiru.label: debated
c-habiru.note: The term was used for many groups across the Near East.

c-tut-restore.text: Under Tutankhamun the court left Amarna and restored the worship of Amun.
c-tut-restore.label: consensus

c-tut.text: Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922; clearing its more than 5,000 objects took about a decade.
c-tut.label: consensus

c-gem.text: The Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza opened fully in November 2025, showing Tutankhamun's objects together for the first time.
c-gem.label: consensus

c-thutmose2.text: In 2025 a tomb west of the Valley of the Kings was identified as that of Thutmose II, the first pharaoh's tomb found since Tutankhamun's.
c-thutmose2.label: consensus

c-ramesses.text: Ramesses II reigned from 1279 to 1213 BCE, one of the longest reigns in Egyptian history.
c-ramesses.label: approx

c-kadesh.text: At Kadesh in Syria, about 1274 BCE, Ramesses II fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II; Egyptian temple reliefs proclaim a great victory, but the Hittites kept Kadesh and historians judge it a draw.
c-kadesh.label: consensus

c-kadesh-armies.text: Britannica estimates the Egyptian advance force at about 20,000 infantry and 2,000 chariots, and the Hittites at about 40,000 infantry and 3,000 chariots.
c-kadesh-armies.label: approx

c-treaty.text: About 1259 BCE Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III made a treaty of peace and alliance; it survives in an Egyptian version on temple walls and an Akkadian version from the Hittite capital.
c-treaty.label: approx
c-treaty.note: A new fragment of the Akkadian version, with clauses protecting returned fugitives and their families, was announced in 2026.

c-treaty-first.text: The treaty is often called the world's first peace treaty; in fact older treaties are known from 3rd-millennium Mesopotamia and Syria.
c-treaty-first.label: consensus
c-treaty-first.note: Cécile Michel lists treaties between Lagash and Uruk, Ebla and Abarsal, and Naram-Sin and Elam, all before 2200 BCE.

c-piramesse.text: Ramesses II built a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the eastern Delta at Qantir; magnetic surveys reveal several square kilometres of buildings.
c-piramesse.label: consensus

c-merneptah.text: A victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah, about 1208 BCE, says 'Israel is wasted, bare of seed', writing Israel with the sign for a people, while Ashkelon and Gezer get the sign for a place.
c-merneptah.label: consensus

c-merneptah-first.text: The Merneptah Stele is generally regarded as the earliest secure mention of Israel outside the Bible.
c-merneptah-first.label: debated
c-merneptah-first.note: Some scholars read 'Israel' on a broken relief in Berlin about two centuries older; most reject the reading on grounds of spelling.

c-exodus-silence.text: No Egyptian text mentions the Exodus or Israelites living in Egypt.
c-exodus-silence.label: consensus
c-exodus-silence.note: Scholars agree on the silence and disagree about what it means: some say royal records omitted defeats and foreign slaves, others that a mass departure would have left traces.

c-exodus-views.text: Scholarly views on the Exodus range from a historical core of the biblical account, to a smaller group (perhaps the Levites) who came from Egypt, to a story composed centuries later with no mass departure behind it.
c-exodus-views.label: debated
c-exodus-views.note: James Hoffmeier argues the Egyptian background supports the tradition; Richard Elliott Friedman argues for a Levite exodus; William Dever sees most early Israelites as people already living in Canaan; Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman see the story as shaped in 7th-century Judah.

c-pithom.text: Where the biblical store-city of Pithom stood is debated, and one candidate site, Tell el-Maskhuta, was unoccupied from about 1500 BCE until about 600 BCE.
c-pithom.label: debated
c-pithom.note: Pithom has been placed at Tell el-Maskhuta or at Tell er-Retaba. Some take the store-city names in Exodus 1:11 to reflect later geography; others, such as Kenneth Kitchen, disagree.

c-exodus-date.text: Those who see a historical Exodus disagree on its date: 1 Kings 6:1 points to about 1446 BCE, while many prefer the 13th century, under Ramesses II.
c-exodus-date.label: debated
c-exodus-date.note: Each date faces difficulties: little evidence of destruction in Canaan around 1400 BCE for the early date; the compressed period of the Judges for the late date.

c-seasons.text: The Egyptian civil year had three seasons, Akhet, Peret and Shemu, each of four 30-day months, plus five extra days: 365 in all.
c-seasons.label: consensus

c-wages.text: Wages were paid in grain, bread and beer, scaled by rank.
c-wages.label: consensus

c-deirmedina.text: Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb-builders, has yielded tens of thousands of written documents, mostly on potsherds and flakes of limestone, from about 1275 to 1075 BCE.
c-deirmedina.label: approx

c-literacy-dm.text: In some periods most men at Deir el-Medina could read and write, against perhaps 1-2 percent of Egyptians as a whole.
c-literacy-dm.label: approx
c-literacy-dm.note: Estimates of literacy are rough; how many women at Deir el-Medina could read is unknown.

c-strike.text: In year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1156 BCE, the tomb-builders stopped work because their rations were late, the first recorded strike in history.
c-strike.label: approx
c-strike.note: The date depends on the chronology used; the Turin papyrus records several stoppages.

c-women.text: Egyptian women could own and sell property, make contracts, go to court and serve as witnesses, and either spouse could end a marriage.
c-women.label: consensus

c-naunakhte.text: About 1145 BCE a woman of Deir el-Medina named Naunakhte made a will before a village court, disinheriting the children who had not supported her in old age.
c-naunakhte.label: consensus

c-medicine.text: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, copied about 1600 BCE, describes 48 cases of injury from head to foot, with a judgement for each; the Ebers Papyrus, about 1550 BCE, has about 700 remedies, practical and magical.
c-medicine.label: consensus

c-daba-ages.text: At Tell el-Dab'a, about 1700-1550 BCE, almost a third of the 257 people buried died by the age of six; adult women died at about 30 on average and men at about 34.
c-daba-ages.label: approx
c-daba-ages.note: One site; estimating age from skeletons is imprecise.

c-kerma.text: Kerma in Sudan was the capital of the kingdom of Kush, about 2500-1500 BCE, a planned city of more than 30 hectares.
c-kerma.label: approx

c-reisner.text: George Reisner, who excavated Kerma in 1913-16, saw it as an Egyptian trading post; Charles Bonnet's excavations from 1977 showed it was the capital of an African state.
c-reisner.label: consensus

c-kerma-tombs.text: Kerma's kings were buried under earth mounds up to about 90 metres across, with rows of cattle skulls, with many people sacrificed in the largest tombs.
c-kerma-tombs.label: approx
c-kerma-tombs.note: Estimates of the number sacrificed range from dozens to several hundred.

c-thutmose-nubia.text: Thutmose I (about 1504-1492 BCE) pushed beyond the Fourth Cataract and set up a boundary inscription at Kurgus; Nubian gold drew Egypt south.
c-thutmose-nubia.label: consensus

c-napata.text: Gebel Barkal near Napata was sacred to Amun from about 1500 BCE and became the religious centre of a revived kingdom of Kush from about 900 BCE.
c-napata.label: approx

c-piye.text: About 728 BCE the Kushite king Piye marched north and conquered Egypt, founding the 25th Dynasty.
c-piye.label: approx
c-piye.note: Dates for Piye's reign differ between sources by several years.

c-taharqa.text: Taharqa (about 690-664 BCE), the Tirhakah of 2 Kings 19:9 (NRSVUE 'King Tirhakah of Cush'; KJV 'king of Ethiopia'), supported the kingdoms of the Levant against Assyria; the Assyrians took Memphis in 671 and sacked Thebes in 664-663, driving the Kushites out of Egypt.
c-taharqa.label: consensus

c-meroe.text: Kush remained a major power at Napata and later Meroë until the 4th century CE; its kings were buried in steep pyramids.
c-meroe.label: consensus

c-sudan-loot.text: Since 2023, during Sudan's civil war, the Sudan National Museum has been looted on a large scale.
c-sudan-loot.label: consensus

c-cambyses.text: The Persian king Cambyses II conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.
c-cambyses.label: consensus

c-alexandria.text: Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 332 BCE; after his death his general Ptolemy made himself king in 305 BCE.
c-alexandria.label: consensus

c-library.text: The Ptolemies founded the Library and Museum of Alexandria in the early 3rd century BCE.
c-library.label: consensus
c-library.note: When and how the Library was destroyed is debated.

c-pharos.text: The lighthouse of Alexandria, completed under Ptolemy II, was at least 100 metres tall and stood until earthquakes wrecked it between the 10th and 14th centuries.
c-pharos.label: approx

c-cleopatra.text: Cleopatra VII ruled from 51 BCE until her death in 30 BCE, when Egypt became a Roman province; Plutarch says she was the only one of her dynasty to learn Egyptian.
c-cleopatra.label: consensus

c-last-hieroglyphs.text: The last known hieroglyphic inscription dates to 394 CE; the language lived on as Coptic, written in Greek letters, and survives in the liturgy of the Coptic Church.
c-last-hieroglyphs.label: consensus

c-kinglists.text: Egyptian chronology is built from king lists such as the Palermo Stone and the Turin papyrus, from Manetho's history written in Greek for Ptolemy II, and from astronomical records.
c-kinglists.label: consensus

c-bronkramsey.text: A 2010 radiocarbon study of 211 samples broadly confirmed the conventional chronology, suggesting that the New Kingdom may have begun a decade or two earlier.
c-bronkramsey.label: approx
c-bronkramsey.note: It placed Djoser's accession at 2691-2625 BCE and Ahmose's at 1570-1544 BCE, against the conventional 2667 and 1550.

c-periods-egypt.text: Egyptologists divide its history into kingdoms and intermediate periods; this book uses the dates of the Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000).
c-periods-egypt.label: approx
c-periods-egypt.note: All dates before 664 BCE are approximate.

pages.title: Egypt
pages.lede: Egypt is a long green ribbon in a desert. The Nile watered it, fed it, carried its trade and set its calendar, and for three thousand years it held one of the most stable civilizations in history.
body: Herodotus, visiting in the 5th century BCE, wrote that Egypt was land 'acquired by the Egyptians, given them by the river', built up from its mud: the origin of 'the gift of the Nile'. [[c-gift]] The Nile is about 6,650 km long, [[c-nile-length]] and almost none of Egypt's water fell on Egypt. Each summer, heavy rains on the Ethiopian highlands swelled the Blue Nile and the Atbara, and the flood reached Aswan in July and peaked near Cairo in October. [[c-flood]] [[c-flood-timing]]

The flood laid down fresh black silt. Egyptians called their country Kemet, 'the black land', and the desert beyond it Deshret, 'the red land'. [[c-kemet]] Everything depended on the height of the water: a Roman writer recorded that a low flood meant famine and a high one 'unbounded transports of joy'. [[c-pliny-flood]]

rows: a strip along the river, and the Delta

body: Egypt had two halves: Upper Egypt, the narrow valley in the south, and Lower Egypt, the broad Delta in the north. They had distinct cultures before they were united, and the king remained 'Lord of the Two Lands'. [[c-two-lands]] How many people lived there is uncertain: one estimate rises from under a million at unification to about three million under Ramesses II. [[c-population]]

body.compare: Compare Mesopotamia (3.0): two rivers, irrigation, little rain. But the Nile flood came at the right time of year for crops and was far more predictable than the Tigris and Euphrates.

The White Nile, from the lakes of central Africa
Winter rains along the Mediterranean coast
Melting snow on the Ethiopian mountains

wrong.2: The flood reached Aswan in July and peaked at Cairo in October; it did not come with winter rain.
wrong.3: The flood came from heavy summer rain, not snow.

practice.q: What do figures like '2.9 million people under Ramesses II' represent?
choices: Totals taken from a census of the whole kingdom
Disputed estimates of what the land could support
A figure that most specialists now agree on
Evidence that Egypt's population shrank over time
practice.why: No count of pharaonic Egypt's whole population survives; Karl Butzer's figures estimate what the land could support, and others estimate 4-5 million for the New Kingdom.

wrong.0: No count of pharaonic Egypt's whole population survives.
wrong.2: Others estimate 4-5 million for the New Kingdom.
wrong.3: Butzer's estimates rise, from about 0.9 million at unification to 2.9 million under Ramesses II.

pages.title: The first kings
pages.lede: Before there were pharaohs there were chiefs, cemeteries and rival centres along the Nile. Within a few centuries they became a single kingdom, with writing, a capital and a king who was buried with his servants.
body: The Naqada culture of Upper Egypt, from about 4000 to 3000 BCE, saw growing towns, rich graves and trade. [[c-naqada]] Radiocarbon dates show the Egyptian state formed quickly: the first king of the 1st Dynasty, Aha, came to the throne about 3100 BCE. [[c-dee]]

Writing appeared at about the same time as in Mesopotamia. In a tomb at Abydos of about 3200 BCE, archaeologists found small bone and ivory labels with signs recording goods and places. [[c-uj]] On the Narmer Palette, about 3100 BCE, the king wears the white crown of the south on one side, striking down an enemy, and the red crown of the north on the other. [[c-narmer]] Whether it records an actual conquest or a statement of royal power is debated; unification probably took several reigns. [[c-narmer-event]] Later Egyptians credited it to a king called Menes, whose identity is unknown. [[c-menes]]

body: The first kings were buried at Abydos, ringed by the graves of servants. A 2026 study found that many of their skulls bear injuries from the time of death: they were killed to serve the king in the afterlife. The practice seems to have ended with the 1st Dynasty. [[c-retainers]]

In 2025 geneticists published the first complete genome from an ancient Egyptian, a man buried around the start of the pyramid age: mostly North African ancestry, with about a fifth from the eastern Fertile Crescent. [[c-genome]]

pages.title: The pharaoh and maat
pages.sub: kingship and the order of the world
pages.lede: The Egyptian king stood between the gods and humanity. His task was to keep maat, the right order of the universe, against the chaos that always threatened it.
body: Egyptians did not call their king 'pharaoh' until the New Kingdom. The word comes from per-aa, 'great house', the palace, much as people today say 'the White House'. [[c-pharaoh-word]] The king had five official names, [[c-titulary]] and was identified in life with Horus, the falcon god of kingship, and in death with Osiris. [[c-horus]]

His central duty was maat: the order of the universe established at creation, and also truth and justice among people. By building temples, making offerings, judging fairly and defeating Egypt's enemies, he held back chaos. [[c-maat]]

How divine was he? Egyptians spoke of him as a god and depicted him among the gods, but scholars debate how literally they meant it: one influential view sees the king as the manifestation of Horus in the palace, a role that made a mortal man more than human while he held it. [[c-divine-king]] After about thirty years on the throne, and then every few years, a king might hold a Sed festival to renew his powers. [[c-sed]]

body.compare: Compare Naram-Sin and Shulgi in Mesopotamia (3.6, 3.7), who claimed divinity in their lifetimes, and the Hebrew Bible's very different picture of kingship (5.9).

Debated: Posener stressed divinity; Frankfort disagreed
Egyptians saw the king as a purely human ruler
Agreed: the king was held to be fully a god

wrong.2: He was identified with Horus in life and Osiris in death.
wrong.3: Scholars disagree; Baines sees the manifestation of Horus in a man whose ordinary status was hardly a god's.

pages.title: The pyramids
pages.lede: In less than a century, Egyptian kings went from the first stone building to the largest stone structure on Earth. The pyramids are monuments to an idea of kingship, and to a state that could organise labour on an enormous scale.
body: Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, about 2650 BCE, is the first pyramid and the first large stone building in Egypt; his official Imhotep is remembered as its architect. [[c-step]] [[c-imhotep]] Sneferu built three pyramids, learning as he went: at Dahshur the Bent Pyramid changes angle halfway up, and the Red Pyramid became the first true pyramid completed. [[c-sneferu]]

His son Khufu built the Great Pyramid at Giza, about 146 metres high, its sides over 230 metres long and almost perfectly equal, made of an estimated 2.3 million blocks. [[c-great-pyramid]] It remained the tallest structure people had built for more than three thousand years. [[c-tallest]] Khufu's son Khafre, who followed the short reign of Djedefre, added a second pyramid and, probably, the Great Sphinx. [[c-sphinx]]

Who built them? Herodotus said Khufu forced 100,000 Egyptians at a time to labour on it. [[c-herodotus-pyramid]] Archaeology tells a different story: a town of workers south of the Sphinx with bakeries, grain stores and barracks, [[c-workers-town]] and a logbook kept by an official named Merer, who shipped limestone by boat from the quarries at Tura to Giza. [[c-merer]] The workers were not slaves but organised, fed and rotated, though their labour was hardly voluntary. [[c-not-slaves]]

Mysteries remain. How the blocks were raised is still argued. [[c-ramps]] A 2024 study mapped a lost branch of the Nile that may have brought boats close to the pyramid fields, [[c-ahramat]] and in 2023 cosmic-ray imaging found a hidden corridor inside the Great Pyramid. [[c-corridor]]

practice.q: What is the strongest evidence that the pyramids were built by organised state labour rather than slaves?
choices: The workers' town at Giza and Merer's logbook
Herodotus's account of 100,000 forced men
The vast size of the Great Pyramid itself
Inscriptions calling the workers volunteers
practice.why: A town of workers with bakeries, grain stores and barracks, and Merer's logbook of shipping limestone from Tura to Giza, point to organised crews fed by the state.

wrong.1: Herodotus wrote two thousand years later and says the workers were forced.
wrong.2: Size shows a state that could organise labour, but not whether the workers were slaves.
wrong.3: The evidence is archaeological, the workers' town and Merer's logbook; Mark Lehner calls the labour obligatory, not voluntary.

practice.q: What does the 2024 'Ahramat branch' study mainly try to explain?

How the blocks were lifted up the pyramid's sides
What the hidden corridor found in 2023 was for
Why Tura limestone was dragged overland to Giza

wrong.1: How the blocks were raised is a separate debate.
wrong.2: The corridor was found by cosmic-ray imaging; its purpose is unknown.
wrong.3: Merer's logbook shows the limestone came by boat.

pages.title: Gods and the afterlife
pages.sub: Osiris, mummies and the weighing of the heart
pages.lede: Egyptians invested more in death than almost any people in history. Their religion promised that the dead, properly prepared and judged worthy, could live for ever.
body: Egypt had hundreds of gods, many linked with animals: Horus with the falcon, Hathor with the cow, Thoth with the ibis, Amun with the ram. [[c-gods-egypt]] Priests at Heliopolis taught that from the creator Atum came eight further gods, among them Osiris, Isis and Seth. [[c-ennead]] Osiris was murdered by his brother Seth, restored by his wife Isis and became king of the dead; but no full Egyptian telling survives, and the fullest version is by the Greek writer Plutarch, about 120 CE. [[c-osiris]]

A person had several spiritual parts, including the ka, a life-force that received food offerings, and the ba, shown as a bird with a human head that could leave the tomb by day. [[c-soul]] Both needed the body, so it was preserved. Embalming took about 70 days, and its quality depended on what a family could afford. [[c-mummification]] Millions of animals were mummified too, as offerings to gods; many wrappings, scans show, contain no animal at all. [[c-animal-mummies]]

body: The texts that guided the dead changed over time. [[c-texts]] In the Book of the Dead, the dead person declares before the gods the sins they have not committed, and their heart is weighed against the feather of Maat; a heavy heart is devoured. [[c-weighing]] Scholars once thought the afterlife began as a privilege of kings and was 'democratised' after the Old Kingdom; many now argue that elites already hoped for it, and what changed was the practice of writing it down. [[c-democratisation]]

pages.title: Writing and scribes
pages.sub: hieroglyphs, and how they were read again
pages.lede: Egyptian writing was beautiful, complex and, for most of history, the possession of a tiny elite. For fourteen centuries after its last use no one could read it, until the Rosetta Stone.
body: Hieroglyphs combined three kinds of sign: signs for sounds, signs for whole words, and 'determinatives', silent signs that showed what kind of thing a word meant. Vowels were not written. [[c-script-types]] Scribes of the Old Kingdom used over a thousand signs, those of the Middle Kingdom about 750, and Ptolemaic priests thousands. [[c-sign-counts]]

Hieroglyphs were for monuments. For daily use scribes wrote hieratic, a flowing hand, and from about 700 BCE demotic, a still faster script. [[c-hieratic]] Writing was rare: perhaps 1 percent of Egyptians could read in the third millennium BCE, though some communities did far better. [[c-literacy]] A Middle Kingdom school text, the 'Satire of the Trades', urged boys to become scribes and escape the miseries of every other job. [[c-satire]]

In 1799 French soldiers found a stone at Rosetta carrying a decree of 196 BCE in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek: three scripts, two languages. [[c-rosetta]] Thomas Young showed that hieroglyphs could spell foreign royal names by sound; in 1822 Jean-François Champollion showed how sound-signs and word-signs worked together, and the script could be read again. [[c-champollion]]

Word-signs and silent signs sat beside sound-signs

Literacy rates are known exactly from census records
The evidence is thin, and literacy varied by place

pages.title: Collapse and renewal
pages.sub: the First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom
pages.lede: After the pyramid age, Egypt fell apart into rival kingdoms for about a century. When it was reunited, its rulers and writers looked back on the collapse as a warning, and produced the classics of Egyptian literature.
body: The Old Kingdom ended after the unusually long reign of Pepi II; contemporary texts record his 62nd and 65th years. [[c-pepi]] In the First Intermediate Period, rival kings ruled from Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south. [[c-fip]] Was drought to blame? Barbara Bell argued in 1971 that the Nile floods failed; Nadine Moeller has argued that the famine texts in tombs are largely boasts of good governance, and that the climate dried gradually. Today she sees drought as one factor among several. [[c-fip-drought]]

A poem, the 'Admonitions of Ipuwer', describes Egypt turned upside down: the poor grow rich, the river is blood. It was long read as an eyewitness account of the collapse, and some popular writers read it as a record of the Exodus plagues. Most Egyptologists now date it later and read it as literature. [[c-ipuwer]] [[c-ipuwer-exodus]]

Mentuhotep II of Thebes, king from about 2055 BCE, reunited Egypt during his long reign. [[c-mentuhotep]] The Middle Kingdom's kings developed the Faiyum basin, [[c-fayum]] and Senusret III fixed the southern border at Semna, guarded by mud-brick fortresses against Kush. [[c-semna]]

pages.title: The Hyksos and the New Kingdom
pages.sub: from foreign rule to empire, c. 1650-1350 BCE
pages.lede: For about a century, kings of Levantine origin ruled northern Egypt. When the Thebans drove them out, Egypt built an empire that reached from Syria to the heart of Sudan.
body: The Hyksos, 'rulers of foreign lands', governed from Avaris in the eastern Delta. [[c-hyksos]] People from the Levant had lived there for generations, many in royal service, and under the Hyksos the town grew to about 250 hectares. [[c-avaris]] A 2020 study of tooth enamel found that many of its people had grown up outside Egypt before the Hyksos took power, suggesting they rose from within rather than invading. [[c-stantis]] The period is usually credited with bringing the horse and chariot to Egypt. [[c-chariot]]

Ahmose of Thebes, king from about 1550 BCE, took Avaris and drove the Hyksos out, beginning the New Kingdom. [[c-ahmose]] His successors turned outward. In his 23rd year Thutmose III defeated a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian rulers at Megiddo after leading his army through a narrow pass; his annals at Karnak tell the story in detail. [[c-megiddo]] At its height the empire reached beyond the Euphrates and south past the Fourth Cataract. [[c-empire]]

pages.title: Hatshepsut and Akhenaten
pages.sub: a woman king and a religious revolution
pages.lede: Two rulers of the 18th Dynasty broke the rules in different ways: Hatshepsut ruled as king, and Akhenaten tried to replace Egypt's gods with one.
body: Hatshepsut, widow of Thutmose II, first acted for her young stepson Thutmose III and then took the full titles of a king, ruling from about 1473 to 1458 BCE. She built the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri. [[c-hatshepsut]] Its walls show an expedition to the land of Punt bringing back myrrh trees, incense, gold and ebony; Punt probably lay in the region of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia. [[c-punt]] Thutmose III later had her images removed, but some twenty years after her death, which makes simple revenge unlikely. [[c-defacement]]

About a century later Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, made the Aten, the disk of the sun, the centre of worship, closed the temples of other gods, and built a new capital at Amarna. [[c-akhenaten]] Whether this was monotheism is debated: the king and queen Nefertiti shared in the cult as the Aten's only intermediaries. [[c-monotheism]] [[c-nefertiti]]

His Great Hymn to the Aten praises the sun as creator of all life, and it has striking parallels with Psalm 104 (compare the plate on the right). Some scholars think the psalmist knew the hymn; others see a shared tradition of praise. [[c-psalm104]]

Clay tablets found at Amarna, mostly letters in Akkadian, record Egypt's dealings with great kings and with vassal rulers in Canaan. [[c-amarna-letters]] The ruler of Jerusalem complained of raids by the Habiru, outlaws and mercenaries; whether the name is linked to 'Hebrew' is debated. [[c-habiru]] After Akhenaten's death the court left Amarna, and under Tutankhamun the old gods returned. [[c-tut-restore]]

pages.title: Ramesses, Kadesh and the Exodus question
pages.lede: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years, built on a colossal scale and fought the Hittites to a standstill. His son's reign gives the earliest secure mention of Israel, and his own is often linked with the Exodus.
body: Ramesses II reigned from 1279 to 1213 BCE. [[c-ramesses]] He built a new capital in the eastern Delta, Pi-Ramesses, [[c-piramesse]] and covered Egypt with temples. Around 1274 BCE he marched north and met the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh in Syria. His temples proclaim a great victory; in fact the Hittites kept Kadesh, and historians judge the battle a draw. [[c-kadesh]] About fifteen years later Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III made a treaty of peace and alliance, preserved in both Egyptian and Akkadian. [[c-treaty]] It is often called the first peace treaty in history; older ones are known. [[c-treaty-first]]

About 1208 BCE, his son Merneptah set up a stele boasting of victories in Canaan, naming places such as Ashkelon and Gezer, and declaring: 'Israel is wasted, bare of seed.' Israel is written with the sign for a people, not a city or land. [[c-merneptah]] It is generally regarded as the earliest secure mention of Israel outside the Bible. [[c-merneptah-first]]

What about the Exodus? No Egyptian text mentions it, or Israelites in Egypt. [[c-exodus-silence]] Scholars read that silence very differently. Some argue the Egyptian background of the story is authentic; some that a smaller group, perhaps the Levites, came out of Egypt; others that the story was composed much later. [[c-exodus-views]] Even the places named are disputed: one candidate for Pithom, Tell el-Maskhuta, was unoccupied from about 1500 BCE until it was refounded about 600 BCE, while Raamses (Exodus 1:11) matches Ramesses II's capital Pi-Ramesses, occupied in the 13th century. [[c-pithom]] Those who accept a historical Exodus disagree on its date. [[c-exodus-date]]

pages.title: Daily life
pages.lede: Most Egyptians were farmers whose year followed the river. The best window on ordinary lives, though, is a village of craftsmen who built the royal tombs and wrote down almost everything.
body: The year had three seasons of four months each, Akhet, Peret and Shemu, plus five extra days at the end. [[c-seasons]] Wages were paid in kind: grain, bread and beer, scaled by rank. [[c-wages]]

Deir el-Medina, near the Valley of the Kings, was home to the workmen who cut and painted the royal tombs. They left tens of thousands of notes on potsherds and flakes of limestone: letters, accounts, laundry lists, love poems and court records. [[c-deirmedina]] In some periods most of the village men could read, against perhaps 1-2 percent of Egyptians as a whole, so the village was not typical. [[c-literacy-dm]] When their rations were late in year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1156 BCE, they put down their tools, sat behind a temple and shouted 'We are hungry': the first recorded strike. [[c-strike]]

Egyptian women had unusual legal rights for the ancient world: they could own and sell property, make contracts, go to court and divorce. [[c-women]] An elderly villager named Naunakhte made a will before a court of her neighbours and cut out the children who had not looked after her. [[c-naunakhte]]

pages.title: Egypt and Nubia
pages.sub: an African rival, and a Kushite dynasty
pages.lede: South of the First Cataract lay Nubia, home to kingdoms that traded with Egypt, fought it, were conquered by it and, in the 8th century BCE, conquered Egypt in turn.
body: Kerma, in what is now Sudan, was the capital of the kingdom of Kush from about 2500 to 1500 BCE, a planned city of more than 30 hectares. [[c-kerma]] The first excavator, George Reisner, took it for an Egyptian trading post; from 1977 Charles Bonnet's excavations showed it was the capital of a powerful African state. [[c-reisner]] Its kings were buried under great earth mounds with rows of cattle skulls, and many people were sacrificed beside them. [[c-kerma-tombs]] Egypt's Middle Kingdom built a chain of forts on the Nile to hold Kush back (4.6).

In the New Kingdom, Egypt struck back. Thutmose I pushed beyond the Fourth Cataract and carved a boundary inscription at Kurgus; Nubian gold paid for much of Egypt's empire. [[c-thutmose-nubia]] Egyptian temples rose in Nubia, and the mountain of Gebel Barkal became a seat of Amun. [[c-napata]]

Then the tables turned. About 728 BCE the Kushite king Piye marched north and conquered Egypt, founding the 25th Dynasty. [[c-piye]] Piye's son Taharqa (about 690-664 BCE), 'King Tirhakah of Cush' in 2 Kings 19:9 (the King James Version has 'Tirhakah king of Ethiopia'), backed the kingdoms of the Levant against Assyria. The Assyrians took Memphis in 671 and sacked Thebes in 664-663, and the Kushites withdrew south. [[c-taharqa]]

pages.title: The long afterlife of Egypt
pages.sub: Persians, Greeks, Romans, and how we date it all
pages.lede: Pharaonic Egypt lasted three thousand years, and it did not end with a single fall. Persians, Greeks and Romans ruled it in turn, its last pharaohs were Greek, and its language survives in a church liturgy today.
body: After the Kushites, a native dynasty ruled from Sais (664-525 BCE) until the Persians conquered Egypt in 525 BCE. [[c-cambyses]] Alexander the Great took it in 332 BCE and founded Alexandria, and his general Ptolemy made himself king. [[c-alexandria]] For three centuries Greek-speaking Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs. They founded the Library of Alexandria [[c-library]] and built the great lighthouse, whose blocks archaeologists are still raising from the harbour. [[c-pharos]] The last, Cleopatra VII, was, Plutarch says, the only one of her line to learn Egyptian; at her death in 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province. [[c-cleopatra]]
Hieroglyphs were carved for the last known time in 394 CE. The language lived on as Coptic, written in Greek letters, and is still used in the liturgy of the Coptic Church. [[c-last-hieroglyphs]]

How do we date all this? Egyptologists divide this history into kingdoms and intermediate periods (see the plate). [[c-periods-egypt]] To date them they combine king lists such as the Palermo Stone and the Turin papyrus, the history Manetho wrote in Greek for Ptolemy II, which gave us the 'dynasties', and records of the stars. [[c-kinglists]] In 2010 a radiocarbon study of 211 samples from dated objects broadly confirmed the conventional dates. [[c-bronkramsey]]
